Paying for advice: an advice-included fund series versus a fee-based series plus a separate fee

How the MER, trailing commission and a separate advice fee add up, why sales tax on the advice fee matters, and how small differences grow over 20 years. Four charts and an editable comparison.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

The central idea

The same fund can be bought with advice paid inside the MER or with advice billed separately. Neither is automatically cheaper: with a 1.95% MER on one side and a 0.85% MER plus a 1% fee and 13% sales tax on the other, the costs are almost identical.

01

What the MER pays for

A mutual fund's management expense ratio (MER) is its yearly cost as a percentage of your investment. It is taken inside the fund before returns are reported, so you never see a bill. It covers portfolio management, administration, legal and audit costs, regulatory filings and—in most advice-sold series—a trailing commission paid to the dealer that services your account. Sales tax on those costs is already included.

Many funds offer the same portfolio in several series. An advice-included series has a trailing commission inside its MER. A fee-based series (often called F series) leaves the trailer out, so its MER is lower, and you pay your dealer a separate advice fee instead—usually a percentage of assets, with GST/HST added. Since 1 June 2022 Canadian rules stop fund companies paying trailing commissions to order-execution-only (discount) dealers, which do not provide suitability advice.

02

Side by side over 20 years

The model invests CAD 100,000 for 20 years at 6% a year before fees. Route one uses an advice-included series with a 1.95% MER. Route two uses a fee-based series with a 0.85% MER plus a 1% advice fee and 13% HST, for an all-in 1.98%. After 20 years the advice-included route is worth about CAD 221,229 and the fee-based route about CAD 217,509—CAD 3,720 less, because the sales tax lifts the separate fee slightly above the trailer it replaces.

Both routes end equal at an advice fee of about 0.93% before tax. At 0.75% the fee-based route would be ahead by about CAD 9,053; at 1.25% it would be behind by about CAD 15,818. Small percentage differences become thousands of dollars because they compound every year.

03

Cost is only part of the comparison

  • Visibility. A separate fee appears on your statement; a trailer is described in the Fund Facts and your annual charges report but is never billed.
  • Tax. CRA allows fees paid to manage non-registered investments to be claimed as carrying charges on line 22100. Fees for RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs and FHSAs, and commissions on buying or selling, are not deductible. The MER inside a fund is not a separate deduction. The model ignores any deduction.
  • Service. Ask what the fee or trailer pays for: planning, reviews, rebalancing, tax-loss work. Two routes at the same price can buy different service.
  • Eligibility. Fee-based programs often have account minimums; check what applies to you.

Regulators expect advisors to consider costs when recommending products, but that does not mean always choosing the cheapest; cost is weighed with other factors.

04

Questions to ask

  • Which series am I in, and what is its MER?
  • How much of that MER is trailing commission?
  • If I moved to a fee-based series, what would the fee be with sales tax, and is it deductible for my account type?
  • Would switching series be treated as a sale for tax purposes in my account?

Fees, series and services vary by firm. Check the Fund Facts and your fee agreement before deciding.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Original 20-year illustration with reader-entered MERs, fees and returns. Fee mechanics from CSA and fund-company investor materials and CRA line 22100. Not the fees of any specific fund or firm. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.   1. Manitoba Securities Commission · Canadian securities regulators adopt ban on trailing commissions for order-execution-only dealers ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026. Trailing commissions to dealers that make no suitability determination are banned from 1 June 2022.

  2. Fidelity Investments Canada · About fees: Management expense ratios explained ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026. Fund-company investor education: the MER is collected at fund level before returns and covers management, administration and distribution costs including trailing commissions.

  3. CRA · Line 22100 Carrying charges, interest expenses and other expenses ↗

    Page dated 20 January 2026. Fees to manage investments are claimable except for registered plans; commissions on buying and selling are not.

  4. CSA · Client Focused Reforms frequently asked questions (December 2023) ↗

    Costs must be considered in suitability, without a requirement to choose the lowest-cost product.
